newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industry leader attacks Kohl tax reform bill.
newsitem.headline: German industry leader attacks Kohl tax reform bill.

text.p: Hans-Olaf Henkel, the chairman of the BDI industry federation, launched a blistering attack on the German government on Sunday for diluting a tax reform bill aimed at providing more incentives to invest in Germany.
The government sees the bill as a key structural reform to reduce the hefty tax burden on companies and encourage them to create more jobs in Germany, where unemployment is about 11 percent.

But Henkel told Welt am Sonntag newspaper the bill finalised by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's ruling coalition of Christian Democrats, Christian Social Union and liberal Free Democrats (FDP) on Friday would drive even more jobs abroad.
"What they agreed in Bonn is a scandal," Henkel said referring to the bill that is due to be presented to the Bundestag lower house of parliament on Thursday.

Henkel was one of a chorus of industry leaders who initally supported the reform but have recently accused the ruling coalition of retreating from their ambitious tax goals by baulking at unpopular, but necessary measures.

"The German government is competing with the red (the opposition Social Democrat) and green (Greens party) tax populists to the detriment of German business. But it is only business that can create the jobs Germany so urgently needs," Henkel told the newspaper.

The tax reform bill, a mixture of eliminating tax write-offs and lowering tax rates, was originally aimed at a net relief of about 30 billion marks for tax payers. It envisages phasing in tax changes in 1998 and 1999.
But the coalition has admitted it may fall short of this after amendments to the bill were finalised on Friday to help plug new holes that emerged in the 1998 and 1999 budgets.

Bonn is struggling to whip its finances into shape in 1997, the crunch year for fulfilling the financial criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU). But its economic data for 1998 are also an important factor in deciding whether it will qualify to join the planned launch of EMU in 1999.

The bill is set to be approved by the lower house of parliament. But facing certain defeat in the Bundesrat (upper house), where the opposition SPD have a majority, it is probably destined for parliamentary mediation from mid-July.

German news magazine Spiegel quoted BASF chairman Juergen Strube as saying that Kohl's government had "lost control" and warned that if Bonn went ahead with the bill in its current form "no one would invest in Germany".

"If Bonn decides to go ahead with plans that increase rather than reduce the tax burden on industry there is going to be trouble," the weekly quoted Hans Peter Stihl, head of the Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT), as saying.
Spiegel also quoted the head of sports car maker Porsche, Wendelin Wiedeking, as dismissing the reforms as "a bad joke", in a report released ahead of publication on Monday.
Industry leaders pointed out that the reform, which set out to relieve business of a total of 6.5 billion marks in tax, would now save only 1.2 billion marks -- a fraction of that.

They also criticised provisions preventing firms from using profits to offset future losses and other tax changes they said would cancel out any of benefits the bill would bring, such as substantial reductions in corporate tax rates.

But the leader of Kohl's junior coalition partner the FDP, Wolfgang Gerhard, said in a weekend interview he was satisfied with the tax bill, saying it was long overdue and was key to boosting Germany's depressed jobs market.

"This is an important incentive for jobs in Germany. We are doing something which other countries have long practised, we are unfortunately late. We could have done it sooner," Gerhard told Germany's N-TV all-news televison station on Saturday.
